entries.claim: Delete eligibility is decided only during evaluation by checking the transcript path once, but the mutating phase never re-validates that precondition before it removes the session rows.
entries.failure_scenario: If a transcript is restored or recreated after `evaluate` names it for deletion but before `apply` runs, `delete_one` still removes the session, metadata, turns and watermark rows even though the transcript is no longer gone. That makes the destructive path diverge from dry-run and can delete a session whose bytes should have been preserved.

counter_evidence.note: Two of the three consequences the scenario asserts are contradicted by the code it cites. (1) The session bytes are NOT lost: delete_one deletes the watermarks row in the same transaction as the session row, and retention/mod.rs:203-206 states the rule the delete rests on - a session whose transcript is on disk is rediscovered by discover::discover on the next hook spawn and re-ingested from offset 0. A restored transcript is therefore re-archived on the next pass, so the transcript check is a do-not-bother filter, not a data-safety precondition. (2) There is no dry-run divergence of the kind described: --dry-run is a separate invocation of evaluate, so any change between it and a later apply is inherent to every dry-run and is not the evaluate-then-apply window this claim names. The claim itself is accurate - apply.rs:165 delete_one re-checks nothing - and the residual harm is real but narrow: the observations rows deleted at apply.rs:177 are the one thing no reingest reproduces (apply.rs:26-31). The window is the microseconds between evaluate and apply inside one retain() call under the ingest lock, on a transcript absent and untouched for at least age_days. Downgraded to low and queued as an open item.
